HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH  CRR No.4624/2019  (Irfan Ansari vs. The State of M.P. & Anr.)
Indore: Dated:- 14/10/2019:-
 Shri A.S. Rathore, learned counsel for the petitioner.
 Shri R.S. Darbar, learned Public Prosecutor for the respondent/State.

entities.text: HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH  CRR No.4624/2019  (Irfan Ansari vs. The State of M.P. & Anr
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: With consent of the parties, the matter is heard finally.
ORDER 1.

Unsuccessful in trial and in appeal, the petitioner, who is held guilty under Section 7(2) r/w Section 16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and is convicted for six months R.I. with fine of Rs.3000/- and in default 2 months R.I. and whose appeal is dismissed, has now come before this Court challenging his conviction and sentence.

The trial Court has convicted the petitioner vide judgment dated 24/02/2016 passed in Criminal Case No.19996/2009 by Special Judicial Magistrate, Municipal Corporation, Indore and his appeal was dismissed vide judgment dated 11/09/2019 delivered in Criminal Appeal No.259/2016 by 12th Additional Sessions Judge,
Indore.

entities.text: Special Judicial Magistrate, Municipal Corporation, Indore
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
2. Facts giving rise to the present petition are that on 17/06/2009, a team constituted by the Collector, Indore comprising Food Inspector Vivek Gangrade visited the establishment of the petitioner namely, Raja Namkeen, 18-B, Chandan Nagar, Indore, which was a proprietorship firm.
The petitioner produced photocopy of license for the year 2009-10.
After giving information in Form No.6 and after disclosing purpose, the Food Inspector purchased samples of packed snacks (namkeen, sev) by paying cost of the same.

Following the due process the samples were sealed and sent to the public analyst, who after analysis submitted report which, in original reads thus:-
(1) Insects, Moulds, Rodent hair & Excreta = Absent (2) Rancid odour & Rancid taste = Absent (3) Test for starch = Positive (by Iodine test) (4) Test for salt = Positive (by silver Nitrate test) (5) Test for Turmeric = Negative (by Beric acid test) (6)
Extraneous colouring matter = Absent (7) Test for Besan = Positive (by Thin layer chromatography) (8) Test for Teora = Negative (by Thin layer chromatography)

(9)

sentences.text: 1 (ii) Baudouin test for sesame oil = Negative Opinion :- and am of the opinion

that the declaration regarding the name and complete address of the Manufacturer and the Manufacturing units, Lot/code/Batch Number which is a mark of identification by which the food can be traced in the manufacture and identified in the distribution and also the date, month and year in which the commodity is manufactured, packed or repacked are not given on the label (packet) of sev (Indorilal Namkeen) which is required as per sub-rule (c)(i), (e), (f) and (I) of Rule 32 of the P.F.A. Rules 1955,
hence, it is a contravention of the above Rules.
Thus the sample is mis- branded under Section 2(ix), (k) of the P.F.A. Act, 1954.
However, the sample contains permitted edible substances.
The sample was in a condition fit for analysis.

3. After examining the statement of Food Inspector and other witnesses and the documents produced and proved by them, the trial Court as well as appellate Court found the evidence produced by the prosecution reliable and convicted and sentenced the petitioner as stated above.

4. Learned counsel representing the petitioner submitted that the appellant was having valid license for manufacturing of snacks like namkeen sev, therefore, he has good case on merit, but he does not want to press the petition on merits.
He only wants to make a submission about the sentence.

Placing reliance on the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court rendered in Nemi Chand vs. State of Rajasthan reported in LAWS (SC)-2016-3-119 and followed by Single Bench of this Court in CRR No.3324/2019 (Purushottom vs. State of MP) order dated 19/07/2019, he only prayed that the sentence of the petitioner be removed by enhancing fine amount as is done by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the wake of subsequent development in the law.

entities.text: Nemi Chand vs. State of Rajasthan reported in LAWS (SC)-2016-3-119
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Relevant paras of the judgment passed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Nemi Chand case (supra) reads thus:-
"2.
It is not in dispute that the charge against the appellant was only of sub-standardization of goods.

Mr. Sushil Kumar Jain, learned senior counsel appearing for the appellant, submits that though the appellant has some prima facie case even on merits, he would be giving up the plea on merits and his only submission is about the sentence which has been imposed by the courts below.
He has, in this behalf, argued that there has been an amendment in the Act by the Central Amendment Act 34 of 1976 whereby Section 16A was added and under the said section, only a fine is leviable.

He has drawn our attention to the judgment of this Court in "T. Barai V. Henry Ah Hoe and Another" [1983 (1) SCC 177] wherein this Court held that since the amendment was beneficial to the accused persons, it can be applied even with respect to earlier cases as well which are pending in the Court.

entities.text: T. Barai V. Henry Ah Hoe and Another" [1983 (1) SCC 177]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In the said judgment, the Court held as under :-
"22.
It is only retroactive criminal legislation that is prohibited under Article 20(1).

The prohibition contained in Article 20(1) is that no person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act charged as an offence prohibits nor shall he be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the Irfan vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 14 October, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/107824319/
2 commission of the offence.

sentences.text: It is quite clear that insofar as the Central Amendment Act creates new offences or enhances punishment HC- NIC Page 4 of 6 Created On Mon Oct 02 03:31:50 IST 2017 R/CR.RA/662/2013 JUDGMENT for a particular type of offence no person can be convicted by such ex post facto law nor can the enhanced punishment prescribed by the amendment be applicable.

But insofar as the Central Amendment Act reduces the punishment for an offence punishable under Section 16(1)(a) of the Act, there is no reason why the accused should not have the benefit of such reduced punishment.
The rule of beneficial construction requires that even ex post facto law of such a type should be applied to mitigate the rigour of the law.
The principle is based both on sound reason and common sense.
This finds support in the following passage from Craies on Statute Law, 7th Edn., at pp. 388-89:
A retrospective statute is different from an ex post facto statute.
"Every ex post facto law...." said Chase, J., in the American case of Calder v. Bull "must necessarily be retrospective, but every retrospective law is not an ex post facto law.

Every law that takes away or impairs rights vested agreeably to existing laws is retrospective, and is generally unjust and may be oppressive; it is a good general rule that a law should have no retrospect, but in cases in which the laws may justly and for the benefit of the community and also of individuals relate to a time antecedent to their commencement: as statutes of oblivion or of pardon.

They are certainly retrospective,
and literally both concerning and after the facts committed.

But I do not consider any law ex post facto within the prohibition that mollifies the rigour of the criminal law,
but only those that create or aggravate the crime, or increase the punishment or change the rules of evidence

Created On Mon Oct 02 03:31:50 IST 2017 R/CR.RA/662/2013 JUDGMENT and apparent difference between making an unlawful act lawful and the making an innocent action criminal and punishing it as a crime."
(3) From the facts of the present case, we have no doubt in mind that the aforesaid judgment squarely applies thereon.
This appeal is, therefore, partly allowed and the sentence imposed upon the appellant is modified by imposing fine of Rs. 50,000/- which shall be deposited within two months with the trial court.
On deposit of the aforesaid amount, the bail bonds furnished by the appellant shall be discharged."

5. The judgment passed by this Court in Purushottom case is as under:-
"8. In view of the citation of Apex Court which squarely covers the present case, it would be in propriety to substitute the sentence of imprisonment and fine with penalty of Rs.50,000/- in respect of offence for misbranding and adulteration.
The applicant shall deposit this amount before the trial Court within a period of two months.
On depositing such amount, his bail bonds shall be discharged.

Presently,
his jail sentence is being suspended so that he can acquire the desired fund of Rs.50,000.

The substantive jail sentence is suspended on furnishing Rs.50,000/-

3 to the satisfaction of the trial Court for his regular appearance before the trial Court on 22/09/2019 and on all other dates given by the trial Court.

sentences.text: 9. Thus it is specifically directed that copy of this order be sent to trial Court with a direction that if the applicant does not deposit Rs.50,000/- within a period of two months from today, then the order of appellate Court shall be revived and he shall suffer the jail sentence as already imposed by the appellate Court.
On deposition of Rs.50,000 by the applicant, the jail sentence and fine amount as prescribed in the impugned order shall stand quashed and returned to applicant.
This criminal revision is disposed of with conviction having been maintained but partly allowed in terms of sentence.
10. At this point of time, learned counsel for the applicant submits that he undertakes to deposit penalty of Rs.50,000/- on or before 09th August, 2019.
In that event, the applicant be released forthwith by the learned trial Court on deposition of penalty of Rs.50,000/-.
Certified copy as per rules."
6. In the present case, no extraneous substance or adulterant was found in the sample.

The charge against the petitioner is not for selling adulterated food article, but the charge is only of violation of the Rules relating to the information regarding manufacturing unit, lot/code/Batch Number, date of manufacture or packing etc. necessary under Sub-rule (c)(i), (e), (f) and (I) of Rule 32 of the P.F.A.
Rules 1955.

The sample was found misbranded as defined under Section 2(ix), (k) of the P.F.A. Act,
1954.
Therefore, following the dictum of the Hon'ble Supreme Court as well of this Court, the prayer of the petitioner is acceded.
7. The conviction of the petitioner under Section 7(2) r/w Section 16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 is maintained, but his sentence of 6 months RI is set aside.
He is imposed fine of Rs.50,000/-.
As and when the fine is deposited, he be released from the custody if not required in any other case.
Fine amount, if any, already deposited be adjusted.
8. With the aforesaid modification, the petition is allowed and is disposed off to the extent indicated herein above.
